prompt: Which setting on the state bucket makes a deleted state recoverable?
hint: Every write keeps the previous one.

choices.text: public_access_prevention
choices.why: That keeps it private; it keeps no history.

choices.text: versioning
choices.why: Right. Noncurrent versions are what the restore used.

choices.text: uniform_bucket_level_access
choices.why: That simplifies permissions; nothing is kept.

choices.text: A lifecycle rule deleting old versions
choices.why: That limits the history; it does not create it.

prompt: Two configurations are given the same backend `prefix` by mistake. What happens?
hint: The prefix is the configuration's address.

choices.text: Terraform refuses the second init
choices.why: Nothing checks; the prefix is just a folder.

choices.text: Each one's apply overwrites the other's state
choices.why: Right. And each plan then proposes to destroy the other's resources.

choices.text: They share it safely, thanks to the lock
choices.why: The lock serialises writes; it cannot make two configurations one.

choices.text: The bucket keeps two files under the same name, one per configuration
choices.why: One name is one object; the second write replaces it.

prompt: Why is the state bucket kept out of the project's general IAM?

choices.text: Reading the state means reading its secrets
choices.why: Right. Every attribute, generated passwords included.

choices.text: Cloud Storage charges more for buckets shared by many accounts
choices.why: Price does not depend on who has access.

choices.text: Terraform refuses to lock a bucket other accounts can read
choices.why: Locking works whoever can read the bucket.

choices.text: Versioning only works on buckets with few readers
choices.why: Versioning has nothing to do with readers.

prompt: What does `Error 412: Precondition failed` mean in the lock message?
hint: How is the lock object created?

choices.text: The service account lacks permission to write the bucket
choices.why: That would be a 403; 412 is a condition on the object.

choices.text: The state file is corrupt
choices.why: The state was not read at all; the lock write failed first.

choices.text: The lock object already exists
choices.why: Right. It is written only if absent, and somebody holds it.

choices.text: The bucket's versioning is off
choices.why: Locking does not depend on versioning.

prompt: Plans fail with the lock error, and the lock's `Who` is the CI runner, created 40 minutes ago. What comes before `terraform force-unlock`?
hint: The lock may be protecting something.

choices.text: Nothing: 40 minutes is long enough to be sure
choices.why: A long apply can take that long; time alone proves nothing.

choices.text: Running the plan again with -lock=false
choices.why: That ignores the lock instead of finding out why it is there.

choices.text: Deleting default.tfstate so the lock no longer matters
choices.why: That is the lost-state accident, caused on purpose.

choices.text: Checking that the CI job is really dead
choices.why: Right. If it is still applying, unlocking lets two writers in.

prompt: A tutorial suggests `-lock=false` for "Error acquiring the state lock" in a pipeline. What is the risk?

choices.text: Terraform runs more slowly without the lock
choices.why: It is faster, if anything; speed is not the problem.

choices.text: Two runs write the state and the second wins
choices.why: Right. One of them silently loses what it recorded.

choices.text: Cloud Storage refuses writes without a lock
choices.why: It accepts them; that is the danger.

choices.text: The state stops being versioned
choices.why: Versioning is the bucket's, unaffected by the flag.

prompt: After the state was deleted, the plan proposed to create both resources. What did that plan mean?

choices.text: The resources had been deleted with the state
choices.why: They were untouched; only the record went.

choices.text: Terraform had lost track of resources that still existed
choices.why: Right. A plan to create what exists is a stop sign.

choices.text: The configuration had changed since the last apply
choices.why: Nothing in the files changed.

choices.text: The emulator had restarted and forgotten them
choices.why: They were still there; the restore showed no changes.

prompt: Why was the newest version of `default.tfstate` the wrong one to restore?
hint: Look at its serial and its resources.

choices.text: The newest version is always the lock, not the state
choices.why: The list was filtered to default.tfstate.

choices.text: It was corrupted by the deletion
choices.why: It was a valid state: an empty one.

choices.text: The plan after the accident wrote an empty state
choices.why: Right. Serial 1 and nothing: restoring it would change nothing.

choices.text: Versions newer than an hour cannot be read
choices.why: There is no such delay.

prompt: In the list of versions, which `serial` held the shop's state as it should be: two resources, after `slow.tf` was removed?
hint: Three resources was the version with slow.tf.

prompt: Why did `terraform state push` need `-force` in the restore?

choices.text: Because the lock was still held by the plan
choices.why: The plan had finished and released it.

choices.text: It replaced a state of another lineage
choices.why: Right. The empty state was a new lineage; -force says you mean it.

choices.text: Pushing to a versioned bucket always requires it
choices.why: Versioning has nothing to do with push.

choices.text: Because the token was fake
choices.why: The emulator never checked the token.

prompt: After an import, why would the google provider still propose to create the price list object?
hint: Not every resource type can be imported.

choices.text: The object was deleted with the state
choices.why: It still existed; the state was the only thing lost.

choices.text: Its import block named the wrong bucket
choices.why: There is no import block for it: the type does not support one.

choices.text: Its resource type has no import at all
choices.why: Right. The only proposal left is to write it again.

choices.text: Objects are always recreated on every plan
choices.why: With its state, the object showed no changes.

prompt: A pull request changes the backend `prefix` from `shop` to `shop-prod`, and its plan proposes to create twelve resources that exist. What is the right reading?
hint: A new prefix is a new, empty state.

choices.text: Twelve new resources were added in the same pull request
choices.why: They exist already; the plan says create because the state is empty.

choices.text: Stop: the state has to be moved, not recreated
choices.why: Right. init -migrate-state moves it; applying would duplicate or fail.

choices.text: Apply: Terraform will find and adopt the existing ones
choices.why: Terraform adopts only through import; apply creates.

choices.text: Approve it: renaming the prefix is cosmetic
choices.why: The prefix is the state's address, far from cosmetic.

prompt: Put the restore of a deleted state in order.
items: List the noncurrent versions of default.tfstate
Read each version's serial and resources
Download the version with the right serial
trap: Pushing the newest version without reading it is the slip: here it was the empty state the plan wrote.

prompt: The block that tells Terraform which real object a resource address is, without creating it, is called `___`.
Which of these leave Terraform proposing to create resources that already exist? Choose all that apply.
hint: Each one leaves an empty state where the old one was expected.

choices.text: The state object is deleted
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The backend prefix is changed without migrating
choices.why: Yes: a new, empty state.

choices.text: The lock is left behind by a killed apply
choices.why: No. Plans are refused, not misled.

choices.text: An old empty version is restored instead of the right one
choices.why: Yes, as the newest version would have been.

choices.text: A noncurrent version is deleted by the lifecycle rule
choices.why: No. The current state is untouched.
